projects.title: MUOS Integration
projects.summary: Brought the Navy's MUOS satellite network into an artillery battalion's communications: the operating procedures, the keying and a same-night cutover from VHF.
projects.metric: Firmware + 3 antenna kits · 4 satellites + spare · provisioning, KMI keys, SOP, cutover

features.name: KMI and EKMS
features.text: MUOS runs on two layers of keys. The network's AES keys (user cover, over-the-air rekey and group cover keys) are generated by a Navy COMSEC custodian, assigned when a radio is provisioned and pushed over the air, then renewed every year. A radio with an expired cover key has to be provisioned again. The Type 1 keys that encrypt the traffic itself (HAIPE for data, SCIP for voice and calls to the DoD phone network) come through each unit's KMI account, the NSA system that replaced EKMS, and are loaded with fill devices. A radio with the right firmware but the wrong or expired key will not join the net. Photo: Marines use a Simple Key Loader to load cryptographic keys onto a Tactical Key Loader during a class, 2026 (U.S. Marine Corps / DVIDS).

features.name: The network
features.text: MUOS works like a cell network in space: 4 satellites plus a spare, with ground stations in Hawaii, Virginia, Australia and Sicily. Even two radios in the same field talk through the ground segment, which also links them to SIPR, NIPR and the DoD phone network. Photo: the MUOS ground station at Wahiawa, Hawaii, which also hosts the network's management facility (U.S. Navy photo by MC2 John W. Ciccarelli Jr.).

features.name: The gear
features.text: No new radio: L3Harris firmware for the AN/PRC-117G (a $75M order in 2019) plus one of three antenna kits, for the halt, on the move or a VRC-114 vehicle mount. The Marine Corps was the first service to field MUOS widely, starting in 2019. Photo: a transmission system operator with 1st Battalion, 2nd Marines sets up a MUOS-capable PRC-117G, Norway, 2024 (U.S. Marine Corps / DVIDS).

features.name: The antenna
features.text: UHF satellite links need a clear view of the sky. Antenna placement, cabling, diplexers and batteries (SATCOM transmits at 20 W) are part of every setup, and each kit has its own procedure in the SOP. Photo: a transmission system operator with 14th Marines sets up a MUOS antenna, Fort Sill, 2026 (U.S. Marine Corps / DVIDS).

features.name: Provisioning
features.text: Unlike VHF, MUOS has to know a radio before it will carry its traffic: a joint provisioning authority approves every terminal and talkgroup, then the network pushes its own keys to the radio over the air. Requests need lead time, so they belong in the plan, not the night before. Photo: Marines configure an AN/PRC-117G during communications training, 2026 (U.S. Marine Corps / DVIDS).

features.name: Procedures and cutover
features.text: Integration means rewriting the PACE plan (MUOS primary for long range, HF as the alternate), writing the SOP, training operators and running MUOS alongside the old network until it has earned trust. Then the cutover, with the fallback still ready. Photo: a radio chief with Alpha Battery, BLT 3/5, 11th MEU, calls for a radio check on a PRC-117G, Camp Pendleton, 2019 (U.S. Marine Corps / DVIDS).

features.name: Working with other units
features.text: A MUOS net works only when every station shares the same provisioning, talkgroup, key and firmware version, whether it is regiment, the supported infantry, aviation, a ship or the Army. Stations still on legacy UHF connect through DISA gateways or a cross-banding radio. Photo: an HMH-361 avionics officer briefs the MUOS Program Office on MUOS for heavy-lift helicopters, MCAS Miramar, 2023 (U.S. Marine Corps / DVIDS).

features.name: Under jamming
features.text: At Steel Knight 20 (December 2019), 1st Marine Division ran MUOS while an Army team jammed its band. Links held with about half the band jammed, and the command post's emissions looked like a single PRC-117G. Photo: 1st LAR Battalion's communications chief sets up a PRC-117G in a combat operations center, Steel Knight 24 (U.S. Marine Corps / DVIDS).

body: MUOS (Mobile User Objective System) is the U.S. military's narrowband satellite communications system and the replacement for UHF Follow-On. The Navy built it, Lockheed Martin is the prime, and the Space Force has run the program since 2023. It reached Marine units as L3Harris firmware and new antenna kits for the AN/PRC-117G radio.
In the desert around Twentynine Palms, VHF line-of-sight often fails, so MUOS became the battalion's primary long-range network for command and fire-support traffic.

Bringing it into a battalion takes more than radios: every terminal has to be provisioned before it can join, keys have to be in place on two layers, the PACE plan and SOP have to be rewritten, and every unit sharing a net has to match on talkgroup, key and firmware.

Key management sits in the middle of the integration. MUOS's own network keys are made centrally and delivered over the air, but the Type 1 keys for the traffic still flow through the NSA's Key Management Infrastructure (KMI), which replaced EKMS around 2018. Each unit's KMI account orders those keys from the net's controlling authority, issues them to operators, schedules changeovers and makes sure they match the radio's provisioning profile.
I wrote the battalion's MUOS standard operating procedures, a detailed account of communications, operations and the MUOS system, while keeping normal operations and field exercises running.
As the battalion's KMI Primary, I handled the cryptographic keying the radios needed to join the network, and installed, operated and maintained MUOS alongside the HF, VHF and UHF networks.
When a last-minute change moved the communications network from VHF to MUOS, I coordinated the shift the same night, delegating to a team of Marines so operations ran on schedule.

body: Hero One is a local, single-operator research workstation. One search takes a company, product, person or place, and every company in view is one click from each page about it.

It is built on free public and open sources and local inference, with no paid data or metered API. Each observation is recorded with its source and the date it became known, so a test of an idea only uses what was public on that date.

Valuation: two- and three-stage DCF, reverse DCF, dividend discount, residual income and peer multiples (P/E, EV/EBITDA, EV/Sales), aggregated as a median with a margin of safety; where the models disagree, that is treated as information. The discount rate comes from CAPM using the live 13-week T-bill, the stock's beta and an equity risk premium, and every fair value lists the inputs it used and where each came from.
Quality and distress screens: Piotroski F-score, Altman Z-score, the Graham number and owner earnings sit beside each valuation.

Risk and statistics: volatility forecasts (EWMA, GJR-GARCH and HAR-RV), hidden Markov regime models and a Monte Carlo scenario engine. Each model opens to its formula, its inputs and its honest limits.

Validation: ideas are tested walk-forward with purged cross-validation, the probabilistic and deflated Sharpe ratios, and the probability of backtest overfitting. A result that only looks good because many variations were tried does not pass.

Research desk: paper portfolio managers each run a $10,000 paper portfolio split across their analysts' thesis sleeves. Each week the analysts propose hypotheses and test them over ten years of point-in-time evidence; a finding is written into the research library only after it passes every check, including a false-discovery haircut, in more than one weekly test.

I audited my own results. The forward record had 349 scored decisions over 35 sessions, a 47.9% hit rate and a session-clustered t-stat of −0.79: no edge. The audit also found three estimator defects that had been producing false positives, including a deflated Sharpe threshold set at the median of pure noise. I wrote the verdict down, retired the trading stack and refocused Hero One on research. No live trading is authorized.
The project began in April 2026 and is in active development.
projects.purpose: Built to do the groundwork of company research in one place: read the filings, see who owns and supplies the business, and test an idea against its full history before forming a view.

projects.title: Deal Delta
projects.summary: A bid/no-bid decision platform for government contracts. It prices what a contract costs to fulfill and compares that with what it pays.
projects.metric: 5 procurement sources · ~12,800 lines of Python · 100+ automated tests

features.name: Opportunity scanner
features.text: Live and cached federal notices in one feed, each showing set-aside status, an ease-of-delivery score from 0 to 100, place of work and days remaining to respond.

features.name: Search workspace

badge.label: filters: agency, NAICS, set-aside, type, window

features.name: Contract playbook
features.text: A working reference for turning a match into a compliant bid: acquisition thresholds, how to mirror winning searches, and treating the solicitation as the operating manual.

badge.label: playbook rules: thresholds, mirror winners, solicitation as manual

features.name: Grant opportunities
features.text: Grants.gov announcements searched separately from contracts, because grants follow a different money model: indirect cost rates and cost share, with no profit.

badge.label: profit: grants pay indirect costs and cost share

body: Deal Delta scans five government procurement sources: SAM.gov, NJSTART, NYC City Record, LA County RAMP and Grants.gov. It merges them into one searchable local cache, and a feed that is down is reported rather than failing the search.

It converts each solicitation's attachments (PDF, Word, Excel and zip packages) into a numbered requirements matrix with the exact quoted words, then tracks sourcing coverage for every requirement: sourced, sourced but unpriced, or never sourced.

AI sourcing agents price the required goods and services. Part numbers are compared exactly, so a different part is flagged rather than assumed equivalent. The platform computes cost to fulfill against award value, with overhead and bid markup as adjustable assumptions.

Pricing is benchmarked against historical USAspending.gov awards at the 25th percentile, median and 75th percentile. The peer set narrows to the closest comparison it can fill, from NAICS, PSC and agency down to governmentwide, and past awards are ranked by how closely their description matches the notice. It is the same discipline as choosing a comps peer set.

A market intelligence console searches 29 datasets with one keyword: awards, awardees, market share and trend analysis, an incumbent finder, and a capture pipeline that weights each pursuit by its stage's probability of winning.
Grants are modeled under federal cost principles in 2 CFR 200: the 15% de minimis indirect rate and no profit. Labor rates from GSA CALC+ are shown as ceilings, never as cost.
I had to learn federal acquisition to build it, from the source documents: acquisition thresholds, NAICS and PSC codes, set-aside programs and the 2 CFR 200 cost principles.
projects.purpose: Built to answer one question before any bid is written: after sourcing every required good and service, is there a margin, and how does the price compare with past awards?

body: Kingdom brings the financial and operating records of a residential portfolio into one system: properties, units, leases, tenants, loans, insurance, taxes and documents.

Every rent payment and bill posts to a double-entry ledger. The books reconcile to the bank, and the system produces a trailing 12-month operating statement, a balance sheet, owner statements and a tax export.
Analytics measure each property on return on equity, cap rate and cash flow, and the portfolio on concentration by city and property type and on debt and refinancing risk.
A local language model, running on my own PC, reads uploaded leases, bills and statements, masks sensitive numbers and queues each document for review before it is filed.
It is written in Python using only the standard library, with a SQLite database and an automated test suite.

Its data also feeds a separate underwriting model: NOI, cap rate, DSCR, LTV, loan amortization tied to the servicer within $0.01, and a max-bid test for acquisitions. That model stays private because it uses real property figures.
Kingdom is where the accounting I studied became daily practice: I built the system around the books I already keep at work.
All screenshots here use fictional sample data, not real properties or tenants.
projects.purpose: Built to replace separate spreadsheets with one system of record, where every rent payment posts to a ledger and every property can be measured on return, cash flow and risk.

experience.description: I managed the battalion's communications security (COMSEC) account in the NSA's Key Management Infrastructure (KMI) for 3rd Battalion, 11th Marines, 1st Marine Division. KMI is the system that replaced the older Electronic Key Management System (EKMS): accounts order, receive, issue, track and destroy cryptographic keys through it, and every encrypted radio net in the battalion, including the new MUOS satellite network, depended on keys from the account. I was selected for the role as a Lance Corporal (E-3); it is normally held by a Sergeant (E-5). Denver's top three strengths are staying calm under pressure, resourcefulness and adaptability. Calm: in a field exercise in 100-degree heat while fire missions continued, several Marines suffered heat stroke and his communications team helped coordinate the medical evacuation without dropping operations. Resourceful: when radios failed from bad crypto keys and heat, he built an improvised cooling chamber from spare gear and set up HF links on copper wire to keep communications up. Adaptive: when techs were sent to the field, he filled in as a technician, network operator and section leader.

Hardest problems Denver has solved: he wrote the battalion's MUOS standard operating procedures while keeping normal operations and field exercises running, and he coordinated a same-night shift of the whole communications network from VHF to MUOS by delegating to a group of Marines. Leadership: as KMI/EKMS manager Denver trained each monthly group of new Marines into operators, led 12+ operators day to day, and led strike groups and simulated strikes in field exercises.
